title: Year one close: the big lookout
hook: the cycle turns on; next year, the rest of the Torah and the prayer book
carry: you kept me alive for this
tomorrow: Year two opens: back in the cycle

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back: every stop in the wilderness, and every stop of this year. Today, the last step of year one.

There's a moment at the top of a long hike when you stop looking at your feet. For hours it was the next rock, the next root. Then the trail opens onto a ledge, and you turn around. The parking lot is a speck. The stream you crossed is a thread. The steep part that nearly made you quit is just a fold in the hill. You walked all that. Jewish tradition has a blessing for a moment like this, a few Hebrew words for simply having arrived.
screen: `EYES ON YOUR FEET.` → `THE LEDGE.` → `A BLESSING FOR ARRIVING.`

segments.voice: Camp one was first words. Shalom: hello, goodbye and peace. The Shema, six words. Shabbat, rest built into the week. A bracha before eating. Tzedakah, giving, from the same root as justice. Teshuvah, return. Camp two, the stories: the world made and called good, Abraham arguing with God about Sodom, Jacob limping away renamed, Joseph, the sea, Sinai, and a portable tabernacle built from the people's gifts. Camp three, the practices: holy time instead of holy place, blessings through the day, the holidays as they came, tefillin, kashrut, and study as prayer. Camp four read the weekly portion closely, fourteen portions from Bereshit to Va'era, and stopped at hail with fire flashing inside it. Camp five went underneath: the sayings of the sages in Pirkei Avot, a taste of Talmud, Hasidic tales, and the Psalms, ending with neshamah, breath and soul. Now the blessing. It's Shehecheyanu, and the Mishnah already knows it: someone who builds a new house or buys new things says it. Today many Jews say it on the first night of a festival, over the first fruit of a season, for new clothes, for a baby, for a milestone. In English it blesses God who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season. No achievement required. You didn't have to climb well. You only had to arrive. And there's no finish line: when the Torah's last word is read, its first is read right after. Next year picks up at the hail, reads the Torah to its last word, and opens the prayer book page by page.
screen: `CAMP ONE: FIRST WORDS.` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `CAMPS FOUR AND FIVE: PORTIONS, DEPTHS.` · `SHEHECHEYANU: KEPT ALIVE, BROUGHT HERE.` · then, large: `YOU KEPT ME ALIVE FOR THIS.`

segments.voice: Let the year pass in front of you like the view from the ledge, and don't grade it: wholehearted days and half-asleep days both led here. If you pray, say Shehecheyanu now, in Hebrew or in English, for having reached this day; if you don't, quietly name one thing that carried you here, a person, a habit, plain stubbornness. Then let the thanks sit in your chest for a while.
Shehecheyanu. Who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season — the blessing for simply having arrived, no achievement required.
Your line: you kept me alive for this. Tomorrow the scroll keeps rolling. See you in year two.

howItsDone: Many Jews say the Shehecheyanu blessing on the first night of a festival, over the first fruit of a season, for new clothes or a new home, and at personal milestones, thanking God for bringing them to this moment.

fork.setup: you've reached something new: the first night of a festival, the first fruit of the season, the end of a long year. what does the tradition do?
options: wait until you've earned it, then celebrate.
say a blessing for simply having arrived.
stay quiet, so as not to jinx it.
fork.reveal: Shehecheyanu: blessing God who kept us alive, sustained us and brought us to this season. arriving is enough.

original.note: Hebrew: who has kept us alive, the key word of the blessing for arriving.

notes: Psalm 118:24 is quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (the KJV reads the same apart from capitalization and punctuation; JPS 1917 may capitalize 'We' after the semicolon as a verse-half); verify exact wording.
Mishnah Berakhot 9:3: one who builds a new house or buys new vessels says 'who has kept us alive...'. Confirm numbering (some editions 9:2/9:3).

The Shehecheyanu is described in paraphrase, not quoted, and the script does not give its full Hebrew text; the practice invites saying it 'if you pray'. Customs listed (first night of festivals, first fruits, new clothes, a baby, milestones) are common Ashkenazi and Sephardi practice; a Keeper may want to note varying customs (e.g. not said for some occasions).
Index carry 'you kept me alive for this' is a first-person play on the blessing's plural 'us'; kept exactly as indexed.
Review checked against day 330's script on disk: its carry 'look how far' and its look-back theme match.
'Shabbat, sometimes called the oldest labor law' softened from a settled claim; the 'oldest labor law' framing is a popular description, not a historical consensus.
Recap of camps and days (Bereshit to Va'era, fourteen portions; camp 5 sections) follows the y1.md outline.
